newsitem.title: UK: BoE's Davies says new super regulator will work well.
newsitem.headline: BoE's Davies says new super regulator will work well.

text.p: Howard Davies, Deputy Governor of the Bank of England and soon to be head of Britain's new financial super-regulator, said on Wednesday the new, all-encompassing watchdog could work perfectly well.

In his first interview since Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown announced supervision of Britain's banks, securities firms and insurance companies would all be handled by a revamped Securities and Investment Board, Davies told Channel 4 television: "I think it can work perfectly reasonably."
The Bank of England -- commonly called the "Old Lady" -- has had responsibility for bank regulation since 1979.

Brown said on Tuesday he was delighted Davies, who will step down from the Bank to take on his new role, had agreed to lead the new "Super SIB". He said it had long become apparent that the existing regulatory system was not delivering the required level of supervision and protection.

Since the Financial Services Act was passed in 1986, hundreds of thousands of people have been missold pensions and two banks under the Bank of England's watchful eye -- BCCI and Barings -- have collapsed.

Sitting next to his boss, Bank Governor Eddie George, in the studio, Davies said the the bringing together of supervision of all the services now offered by banks -- securities and investment banking for example -- was an "unambiguous plus."

Earlier, George said the move was logical at some point given that the functions of Britain's financial institutions were becoming increasingly blurred -- banks offer insurance and securities services and vice versa. "But we're not confident that point has been reached now."

He repeated that assertion to Channel 4 but said the new system need not be dangerous. "We wouldn't have made that change right now but it's a perfectly reasonable change to make in anticipation of the continuing evolution of the system.
"The important thing right now...is that we should be seen to make it work."
George said the fact his deputy would head the new "Super SIB" would help the necessary flow of information flow between the Bank and the Board.

"You've got to make very certain that the coordination and information flow between the two organisations is extremely close," he said. "The helpful thing...is that the banking supervision in the new super SIB will be conducted largely by Bank staff and headed by the Deputy Governor."

Davies, who was in Argentina when Brown dropped his latest bombshell on Tuesday, explained that the Bank would continue to look at the systemic stability of the financial system as a whole while the SIB would look at the soundness of individual institutions.
And George put a brave face on the latest loss of responsibility for the central bank, saying other countries operated the same regulatory structure.

"Others can make it work, I'm quite confident we will be able to make it work," he said. "But there has to be an interrelationship between the supervisor of the institutions and the central bank with its responsibility for the system as a whole. That is vital and Howard and I agree about that."
George said he had been aware that changes were afoot but had been surprised about the timing.

The Bank has already been stripped of control of the gilt market and government debt auctions and now has lost much of its regulatory role. In return, Brown has given it operational independence to set interest rates.
Bank officials were reported to be less than pleased with the latest overhaul but George denied, to Channel 4 and to reporters earlier on Wednesday, that he had seriously thought about resigning.
